proof:
# Identical residue masses, different exact oblique depths

For n=d=1 and 0<=h<=1/4, let C_h be the convex hull of the three fibers

z=-1: [-1/2,1/2],
z=0: [h-3/4,h+3/4],
z=1: [-1/2,1/2].

These are exactly the integer fibers of C_h. Its projection is [-1,1]. The middle interval contains the average endpoint interval [-1/2,1/2] precisely for the specified h range, so taking the convex hull does not enlarge the prescribed middle fiber. C_h is a full-dimensional convex body.

All these bodies have the same fiber masses (1,3/2,1), total M=7/2. Consequently their entire tables of residue-class masses and largest fiber masses, at every integer modulus, are identical. They also lie in the non-heavy regime: 3/2<M/2=7/4.

Nevertheless their exact maximum normalized depths are

max_{y in S_h} depth(y)=1/2-h/7.

Here is a direct computation. A candidate in the middle fiber is (0,x). Every nonvertical halfspace through it can be written, after positive scaling, as either

t+alpha z>=x or t+alpha z<=x.

For the first orientation, minimize over alpha the total length captured from the two endpoint fibers. Their two thresholds are x+alpha and x-alpha. The minimum sum of their upper-tail lengths is

F_+(x)=min(1,max(0,1-2x)).

To verify this formula, each tail has length clamp(1/2-threshold,0,1). Their untruncated lengths sum to 1-2x. If both can be simultaneously between zero and one, their sum equals this value; moving one threshold far upward and the other downward gives total one; when x>=1/2 both thresholds can be at least1/2 and the total is zero. These cases give the stated minimum. Reflection gives F_-(x)=min(1,max(0,1+2x)) for lower-tail cuts.

Thus the unnormalized depth in the middle fiber is the minimum of

U(x)=h+3/4-x+F_+(x),
L(x)=x-h+3/4+F_-(x).

The halfspaces with zero continuous normal have mass at least5/2 and do not lower this minimum. For 0<=x<=1/2,

U(x)=h+7/4-3x,
L(x)=7/4-h+x.

Their minimum is maximized at x=h/2, with value 7/4-h/2. For x<=0, L(x)<=7/4-h, which is no larger. For x>=1/2, U(x)=h+3/4-x<=h+1/4, also smaller. Therefore this is the maximum over the middle fiber.

At either endpoint integer fiber, a halfspace can isolate that fiber and take its smaller interval tail, so every candidate there has unnormalized depth at most1/2. The global maximum is consequently 7/4-h/2. Dividing by M=7/2 proves the formula.

At h=0 the maximum is1/2; at h=1/4 it is13/28. This is not a counterexample to OC. It shows exactly that residue mass/maximum-fiber invariants alone discard information relevant to oblique depth, so additional geometric or cap-profile information is required to recover the exact depth behavior.
